title: Bench harness: thermal & GPU-clock sweep playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for a class of throughput experiments we haven’t centralized: how GPU thermal state and clock/power policies impact long-run throughput repeatability. The goal is a reproducible harness pattern that combines: (1) controlled GPU clock/power sweeps, (2) client-side pacing & seed hygiene, and (3) observability anchors that let us explain drift vs. noise.

Why this matters (short):
- We see subtle throughput regressions after long runs that correlate with temperature and clock governor changes.
- Standard warmups (token-only priming) don't always expose slow drift due to thermal throttling or scheduler interactions.
- Customers care about sustained throughput guarantees for Reserved/Dedicated SKUs.

Quick summary of approach:
1) Define occupancy anchor points (20%, 50%, 80% occupancy by token/time) for a target model/seq-length mix.
2) Sweep GPU clocks/power in steps (baseline -> +10% -> -5%) and hold each step long enough to reach thermal steady-state.
3) Use a repeatable loadgen config with explicit RNG seeds, synthetic prompt bank, and pacing windows to decouple client-side jitter from device thermal behavior.
4) Capture telemetry: per-worker GPU clocks, frequency stats, power, SM utilization, PCIe transfer stalls, nvml temps, OS CPU steal, OOM/killer events, runtime thread contention counters.
5) Analyze throughput vs. time slices and annotate transitions where clocks/power/policy toggles occurred.

Experiment matrix (example):
- Model: redwood-1-small (8B), seq len 512; payload distribution: 60% short (<=64), 30% medium (65-256), 10% long (257-512)
- Batch strategy: dynamic batching with max_batch_tokens=8192, batching window=8ms
- Occupancy anchors: 400 tok/s (low), 1200 tok/s (med), 2400 tok/s (high)
- Clock steps: default, +100 MHz, -150 MHz (or via power limit steps 250W -> 220W -> 200W)
- Hold time per step: minimum 20 minutes after stability criteria met (variance <3% over 5min window)
- Repeat: 3 full sweep runs per hardware instance (different RNG seeds)

Load generator config guidelines (repeatability-focused):
- Use deterministic prompt bank: hashed prompts -> tokenized -> deterministic sampling off. No temperature sampling during bench.
- RNG/entropy hygiene: set loadgen seed in two places: client request permutation seed and per-session token-sampling seed; record both in trace metadata.
- Client pacing: implement token-window pacing (send bursts that sum to N tokens then wait for window) instead of naive requests/sec to avoid bias from varying response sizes.
- Jitter injection: add a small randomized jitter (0-5ms) to inter-burst gap to break lockstep across clients; keep jitter seedable for repeat runs.
- Session reuse policy: explicit toggles in test plan (cold sessions vs. session-reuse primed for X minutes) and measure KV cache hit fraction.

Warmup and priming recommendations:
- Two-phase warmup: (A) quick priming (3-5 minutes of low-intensity traffic to populate kernels & caches), (B) occupancy ramp (10–20 minutes ramping occupancy to anchor level using the same workload mix).
- Seedless priming variant: when seed hygiene is required, use deterministic prompts but randomized ordering across shards to avoid content-localized micro-thermal hotspots.
- Thermal precondition: run device power soak step (a short synthetic compute-only kernel sequence) to bring GPUs to baseline temperature when comparing clock steps across instances. Record precondition profile.

Stability criteria & stop conditions:
- Consider a run stable when throughput variance <3% across five consecutive 1-minute windows and GPU frequency variance <2% over same interval.
- Abort step if anomalous events appear (OOM, driver reset, PCIe error, kernel crash) and mark run as failed for that instance.

Observability and signals to capture (minimum):
- nvml: clock current, clock sm, memory clock, temperature, power draw, power limit
- Metrics from runtime: per-request latency (p50/p95/p99), tokens/sec, batch-size distribution, batch wait time, KV cache hits/misses, sequence-length histogram
- OS: CPU usage, irq count, irqbalance changes, c-state/pcie-link-state changes
- Tracing: attach request-id -> loadgen seed -> session id mapping for postmortem reproducibility

Common failure modes we saw (notes):
- Unexpected DVFS governor jump caused by OS background job (e.g., irq rebalance) -> introduces 7–12% throughput drop after 30+ minutes.
- PCIe retrain / link negotiate on errant PCIe event -> large tail latencies and throughput collapse until reset.
- Batching wheel-up artifacts where early batches are larger until queue equilibrium reached; obscures per-step stability measurement unless occupancy ramp used.

Data artifacts and how to store them:
- Store raw time-series at 1s granularity for all NVML and runtime counters for 24 hours around the run window.
- Also store summarized slice files: 1-min aggregates and per-step snapshots. Name pattern: run-<model>-<instance>-<seed>-<timestamp>.tar.gz
- Keep the loadgen config (json/yaml) and the exact commit hash of the harness and runtime used.

Analysis playbook (quick):
1) Plot tokens/sec vs. time with vertical markers for clock/power step transitions.
2) Overlay GPU temperature and frequency; look for lag between temp change and frequency stabilization.
3) Correlate batch-size distribution to throughput dips to separate batching artifacts from thermal effects.
4) If throughput drift occurs without clock change, check OS-level events and PCIe logs.
5) Use pairwise comparison across instances with identical config to separate hardware-specific variance from harness issues.

Practical tips and gotchas (warts):
- Don’t rely on single-run stability assertions. Two out of three sweeps should produce consistent directionality; if not, escalate to SRE infra to check node-level firmware/driver differences.
- GPU clocks reported by NVML can be inconsistent during transitions; complement with perf counters and runtime kernel-reported clocks where possible.
- Cloud environments sometimes impose power caps silently (host-level policy). Record instance host metadata and fabric policy tags.

Short TODOs for follow-up work:
- Add an automated thermal precondition step to the harness that records precondition audio/temperature trace for later QA.
- Integrate PCIe event scraping into the experiments pipeline and map to run metadata.
- Build a dashboard template that ingests run artifacts and auto-annotates potential thermal-triggered regressions.

Experiment example (copyable checklist):
- [ ] checkout harness@commit 8b4f3d
- [ ] upload prompt-bank v2025-09-11 -> record hash
- [ ] set loadgen seeds: client=12345, perm=54321
- [ ] precondition: synthetic soak 3min @ 80% SM usage
- [ ] run occupancy anchor low -> hold 25m -> run clock +100MHz -> hold 25m -> run clock -150MHz -> hold 25m
- [ ] collect tarball, annotate run metadata, run analysis script

Notes to self / open questions:
- What’s our desired tolerance for long-run throughput guarantees for Dedicated customers? Use this playbook to derive SLA margins.
- Can we automate detecting host-level power management policy and tag runs automatically?

References & links:
- Internal PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/bench-harness/pull/412 (thermal probe scaffolding)
- Confluence draft: RI/infra/thermal-benchmarking (WIP)
- Example JIRA: JIRA-RI-1782 (thermal sweeps failing on G5x hosts)

If helpful I’ll turn this into a short runbook script and a dashboard template next week. This doc is intentionally concise — I want quick iteration and fast validation on 2–3 host types before we formalize the full protocol.
